answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any disruption from switching primary vendors carries outsized delivery risk right as the contract expires in 14 days. Memory_c2 shows the low-cost vendor can cut costs, but that data point doesn't address risk under a no-slack production schedule, and switching under time pressure is inherently riskier than staying with a known-stable incumbent. Memory_c4 indicates that renegotiating at renewal previously recovered real margin and improved terms without disrupting integration, and memory_c1 confirms the incumbent relationship has been stable across cycles. Given the primary objective is minimizing TCO without increasing delivery risk, attempting an aggressive renegotiation with the incumbent — using the low-cost vendor quote as leverage — addresses the cost mandate while preserving continuity. If the incumbent cannot meet the 18% target, the next cycle can revisit switching or second-sourcing with more lead time. I verified memory_c4 because it's the direct precedent for this action's expected outcome and its reliability matters most before committing capacity this cycle.
